strengths: Novel and underexplored direction: introducing visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) as an interaction modality for embedding models, complementing text-only instruction following; the combination of SAM2 with a VLM embedder is a sensible and well-motivated design that preserves both entity-level and global context.

Comprehensive evaluation on MMEB (36 tasks, both IND and OOD) with consistent gains over strong baselines (e.g., +5.1 points for 2B, +2.0 for 7B), including a careful controlled comparison against VLM2Vec with the same training schema and backbone, which isolates the contribution of the segmentation streamline.

Introduction of a new large-scale benchmark (SCaR, ~1M samples) for visual-interactive retrieval, with a reasonably thorough data pipeline (structured GPT-4V generation, WordNet-based synonym filtering, LLM verification, human inspection of the eval set) and detailed statistics showing negatives are not trivially separable by length or lexical artifacts.

Extensive supplementary experiments: seven ablation variants, hyperparameter studies, catastrophic-forgetting analysis after SCaR-train finetuning, qualitative case studies (in-the-wild I2I retrieval, on-the-fly correction), and re-evaluation of baselines with +SCaR-train finetuning to strengthen fairness.
Well-written, clearly structured, with detailed implementation configurations supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity concerns for SCaR: all ground-truth captions and negatives are GPT-4V-generated (fully generated for ADE20k), so the benchmark may encode GPT-4V biases and stylistic artifacts; the near-zero scores of strong models like GME (5-7%) raise questions about whether the task is genuinely this hard or whether the generated negatives/captions contain systematic distributional quirks that disadvantage off-the-shelf embedders and favor models finetuned on the same GPT-4V-generated distribution.

Baseline fairness on SCaR is asymmetric: baselines cannot natively consume visual prompts and must rely on textualized bounding boxes or cropping, so the large reported gaps (15-20%) partly measure input-format compatibility rather than pure representational quality; the ablation showing |S|=1024 substantially improves SCaR (35.1 vs 30.4) yet the authors retain 256 introduces a mild inconsistency in reported headline numbers.

The architectural contribution is largely a combination of existing components (SAM2 + Qwen2-VL + LoRA + InfoNCE) with a new connector; the scientific novelty rests mainly on the new capability and benchmark rather than methodological innovation.

Added inference/training cost of the segmentation streamline is not quantified (latency, memory vs. VLM2Vec); 74-189 hours on 8xH100 plus a dual-encoder forward pass may limit practicality, and the compute-vs-gain tradeoff against stronger baselines like UniME (+2.0 points at 7B) is modest.

Training relies on uniformly sampled points as a surrogate for visual prompts in non-interactive tasks, which is somewhat ad hoc; the claimed universality would be more convincing with analysis of robustness to point placement and to visual prompts of varying quality.

Reproducibility is only partial at review time (code and 'partial' benchmark samples in supplementary; full release promised), and human inspection details for the 47k-sample eval set (inspector agreement, ambiguity criteria) are not quantified.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored direction: equipping embedding models with visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) rather than text-only instructions. The idea of fusing SAM2's prompt-conditioned segmentation features with a VLM's global embeddings is well-motivated and clearly articulated.

Comprehensive evaluation on the standard MMEB benchmark (36 tasks) shows consistent state-of-the-art results at both 2B and 7B scales against many relevant baselines (GME, LamRA, VLM2Vec, MMRet, UniME), in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution settings.

The ablation study is unusually thorough: backbone choice, instruction usage, resolution, segmentation vs. cropping vs. learned prompter, SAM2 size, connector architecture, embedding length, LoRA rank, batch size, and number of sampled points. The comparison against Prompter (CLOC-style) and Cropped variants specifically supports the claim that segmentation-derived entity features are the source of the gains.

The SCaR data construction pipeline is documented in detail (prompt templates, multi-stage LLM + WordNet + human filtering), and the statistical analyses (word clouds, sentence-length distributions) attempt to rule out trivial shortcuts such as caption-length cues.
Additional analyses such as catastrophic forgetting after SCaR-train finetuning (Table 7) and qualitative examples add credibility to the robustness claims.
weaknesses: Core dependency on GPT-4V-generated data weakens the benchmark's validity: ground-truth captions for some datasets are generated by GPT-4V, and all negative distractors are produced by GPT-4V element-swapping from a rigid <object><relation><scene> template. This systematic, template-driven generation risks introducing detectable artifacts and stylistic biases that models finetuned on SCaR (especially VIRTUE) could exploit. The quality assessment for the training split is indirect (train-and-evaluate), and human inspection covers only the evaluation split.

The evaluation protocol has a self-serving structure: the authors both construct SCaR and train on it, then evaluate on its 'validation' set (there appears to be no held-out test set). Because source datasets (RefCOCO+, VisualGenome, COCO) overlap heavily with MMEB grounding data and with VIRTUE's segmentation pipeline (SAM2), VIRTUE has structural advantages over baselines that cannot consume visual prompts; comparisons where baselines receive only textualized bounding boxes are inherently asymmetric, and the +SCaR-train gains for VIRTUE may partly reflect shortcut learning rather than genuine visual-interactive reasoning.

Absolute SCaR numbers are low and the story is muddy: without SCaR-train, VIRTUE-7B reaches only 27.8% (vs. ~10% random) and GME/LamRA are at 6-7%, i.e., below random-free guessing levels. This raises questions about benchmark noise/difficulty calibration, and the claimed '15.2%-20.3%' improvements in the abstract are mostly driven by the +SCaR-train setting where the benchmark's own training data is used.

Methodological novelty is moderate: the approach is essentially connecting a frozen SAM2 to a frozen Qwen2-VL via a Conv2D+MLP connector with InfoNCE finetuning, following the established VLM2Vec recipe. Region-aware embedding/grounding with segmentation models has been explored (e.g., CLOC, which the authors could not reproduce), so the contribution is more an engineering combination plus a benchmark than a fundamentally new learning principle.

Only precision@1 over 10 candidates is reported for SCaR; richer metrics (recall@k, per-negative-type breakdown) and an analysis of which swap types drive the gains would substantiate the compositional-reasoning claims. The in-the-wild I2I experiments (Sec. E.4.1) are anecdotal (six ground-truth images via Google Search API) rather than a controlled evaluation.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence: e.g., attributing VIRTUE's MMEB advantage over VLM2Vec purely to 'entity-level information' ignores the added segmentation branch parameters, extra input sequence length, and SAM2 pretrained knowledge, which the ablations do not fully disentangle.

The reproducibility statement is incomplete (a release URL is missing in the footnote), and only partial SCaR samples are provided in supplementary materials due to file size, which limits verification of the benchmark's quality claims.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated direction: VIRTUE is among the first embedding models to natively ingest visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) by integrating a segmentation model (SAM-2) with a VLM, a capability absent from prior VLM-based embedders (GME, LamRA, VLM2Vec, UniME).

Strong empirical results on the standard MMEB benchmark: VIRTUE-2B (+5.1 avg) and VIRTUE-7B (+2.0 avg) beat all existing baselines across all four meta-tasks and in both IND/OOD settings, with same-backbone comparisons (Qwen2-VL) isolating the effect of the segmentation streamline.

Introduction of SCaR, a new large-scale (1M samples, 5 source datasets) visual-interactive retrieval benchmark filling a genuine gap, with a carefully documented generation pipeline (element-swapping negatives, WordNet synonym checks, LLM+human filtering) and useful distribution analyses (word clouds, sentence-length statistics).

Extensive ablations (VLM backbone, instructions, resolution, segmentation alternatives, SAM-2 size, connector design, embedding length) and hyperparameter studies that credibly support design choices; the ablation vs. Prompter/Cropped variants is particularly informative.
Thorough analysis of catastrophic forgetting after SCaR-train finetuning (Tab. 7), showing baselines degrade severely while VIRTUE remains stable — a valuable and somewhat surprising finding.
Good reproducibility posture: detailed configuration tables, released code/checkpoints promised, prompt templates for data generation included in full.
weaknesses: Benchmark validity concerns for SCaR: both ground-truth captions and all negatives are generated by GPT-4V, and the three-part <object><relation><scene> template makes negatives highly patterned and systematically detectable (e.g., single-element swaps). VIRTUE, trained on this exact distribution for +SCaR-train, may exploit these regularities rather than genuine region-in-context reasoning; without SCaR-train the 7B gain over UniME is only +1.5, so the headline 15.2%-20.3% claim rests largely on finetuning on the authors' own generated data.

Potential train/test overlap and leakage: SCaR evaluation draws from RefCOCO+/RefCOCOg/COCO-Stuff/VisualGenome/ADE20K, several of which overlap with MMEB-train visual grounding data used to produce VIRTUE checkpoints; 'in-domain' vs 'out-of-domain' for SCaR is not cleanly disentangled, and the evaluation split is only 47k of the advertised 1M samples.

Baseline treatment on SCaR is somewhat artificial: since no baseline natively accepts visual prompts, they receive textualized bboxes ('Referring object bbox: {bbox}') — a format none were trained on — making the comparisons favorable to VIRTUE; the paper does not test stronger alternatives such as prompting a VLM to caption the region, or fine-tuning baselines with bbox-in-text formats for longer than 1k steps.

The use of N uniformly sampled points as a 'surrogate' prompt for non-interactive tasks is ad hoc and its benefit mechanism is not well analyzed (why should 9 random points yield entity-level cues that improve classification/VQA by ~5 points?); the claimed universality gains may partly stem from extra capacity/inputs rather than entity grounding.

Absolute SCaR accuracies are low (27.8%-30.4% without SCaR-train, near the 10% random baseline), and quality control of GPT-4V ground-truth captions relies on self-verification plus limited human inspection; error rates of the generated labels are not quantified.

Some writing/presentation issues: typos ('VIRUTE', incomplete release URL in footnote 1), the central contributions are framed as three 'novelty' bullets, and heavy dependence on GPT-4V is acknowledged but the associated bias risks are not deeply analyzed.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated direction: introducing visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) as an interaction modality for embedding models is an unexplored area, and the paper clearly articulates the core challenge (entity-aware retrieval while preserving global scene context).

New large-scale SCaR benchmark (1M samples) with a careful multi-stage curation pipeline (GPT-4V generation, WordNet-based synonym filtering, dual human inspection with reported Cohen's Kappa of 0.89 and inter-annotator statistics), plus prompt templates fully disclosed in the appendix.

Strong empirical results: state-of-the-art on 36 MMEB tasks (64.8 for 2B, 68.6 for 7B) and large gains on SCaR, with the ablation showing that segmentation embeddings (uniform points) are the source of the MMEB gains relative to VLM2Vec under an identical training scheme—a well-controlled comparison.

Extensive analysis: ablations over backbones, resolution, SAM-2 size, connector design, embedding lengths, and cross-modal alternatives; hyperparameter studies; robustness analysis to noisy/misaligned prompts; points-vs-random-box controls to verify the model actually uses visual prompts; latency/memory analysis; and catastrophic-forgetting reevaluation of MMEB after SCaR-train.
Good reproducibility posture: code, models, and benchmark released; detailed configurations (Tab. 6), ethics, LLM-usage, and broader-impact statements provided.
weaknesses: Benchmark–method entanglement: SCaR is designed by the authors, and VIRTUE's visual-prompt streamlining is naturally aligned with its query format, while baselines must rely on textualized bounding boxes, cropping, or red circles—arguably weaker surrogates. This raises fairness concerns about the headline 15.2%–20.3% SCaR gains; the comparisons are partially mitigated (+SCaR-train baselines) but the zero-shot SCaR gap partly reflects input-format asymmetry.

Architecture is a relatively straightforward composition of existing components (SAM-2 feature map + Conv2D/MLP connector + frozen Qwen2-VL with LoRA and InfoNCE); the technical novelty is incremental, with the main value in the empirical demonstration and the benchmark.

SCaR captions and negatives are largely GPT-4V-generated, including ground-truth captions for some datasets; despite the filtering pipeline, residual model-generated biases/annotation artifacts could influence results, and the training-set quality is only assessed indirectly.

SCaR covers only image-to-text retrieval with bounding boxes; interactive image-to-image retrieval is relegated to qualitative case studies, so the claimed generality of 'visual-interactive embedding' is only partially validated.
MMEB gains at 7B are modest (+2.0 over UniME-7B), and the added SAM-2 stream increases inference cost and memory; the efficiency trade-off is only briefly quantified.

Some claims (e.g., 'consistently achieves state-of-the-art') rely on comparisons where baselines were trained only on MMEB-train while VIRTUE benefits from the newly introduced SCaR data in the +SCaR-train setting.

strengths: Timely and clearly motivated problem: extending embedding models with visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) as an interaction channel is a relatively unexplored direction, and the paper articulates the crop-vs-prompt tradeoff well.
Comprehensive evaluation on MMEB (36 tasks, IND/OOD) against a large set of recent CLIP-based and VLM-based baselines, with consistent state-of-the-art results at both 2B and 7B scales.

Extensive ablations (Tab. 9) covering backbone, instructions, resolution, segmentation alternatives, SAM-2 sizes, connector design, and cross-modal alternatives, plus robustness analyses (jitter, partial masks, off-by-k pixels) and latency/memory analysis.

The segmentation streamline appears to provide genuine benefits on non-interactive tasks (VIRTUE vs. VLM2Vec uses the same training recipe/data), suggesting entity-level representations complement global embeddings.

Reasonably careful benchmark construction pipeline for SCaR with multi-stage filtering (heuristic rules, LLM verification, WordNet checks, human inspection) and reported inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa 0.89), plus code/models/benchmark release. Ethical statements and LLM usage disclosure are present.
weaknesses: SCaR is largely GPT-4V-generated: ground-truth captions (especially for ADE20k) and all negatives come from a single closed-source model. This raises concerns about annotation noise, systematic LLM artifacts, and reproducibility of the benchmark; the quality control for the 957k training samples is only 'indirect' (by downstream performance), which risks training on mislabeled data.

Potential train/eval leakage: the SCaR evaluation sets are built from datasets (RefCOCO+, VisualGenome, COCO-Stuff, ADE20k) whose images and grounding-style content also appear in MMEB-train, on which all compared models (including VIRTUE) were finetuned. The paper does not analyze or rule out this overlap, which weakens claims about generalization on SCaR.

The most important comparison is under-powered: without SCaR-train, VIRTUE-7B's advantage on SCaR over the best finetuned baseline (UniME-7B) is only +1.5 points (27.8 vs. 26.3), far from the headline '15.2%-20.3%' figure; most of the reported gain materializes only after finetuning on the authors' own training set. Headline claims thus overstate the out-of-the-box visual-interactive advantage.

Unfair-ish baseline setup on SCaR: baselines receive only textualized bounding boxes while VIRTUE receives native visual prompts; the crop-based alternative underperforms, but no baseline is adapted to genuinely consume region information (e.g., region-capable models like Ferret/Osprey/CLOC-style architectures), so the comparison conflates interface design with capability.

Internal inconsistencies reduce confidence: Tab. 7 reports 'both annotators flagged' = 4021 (7.7%) but 'either flagged' = 1638 (3.1%), which is logically impossible as stated (either-flagged should be larger); the abstract and reproducibility statements contain blank URLs; Fig. 4 plots lack numeric labels, and Tab. 5's SCaR-train 'w/o all' setting (43.4) is higher than 'w/o inference' (41.9) without explanation.

Scope is narrower than the framing suggests: SCaR only covers image-to-text retrieval with bounding boxes; interactive I2I is relegated to small qualitative case studies (Sec. E.4.1) with ad-hoc GPT-4o/Google-search construction, so the central claim of general 'visual-interactive embedding' is validated on essentially one task family.

Significance of MMEB gains is modest in places (+2.0 overall for 7B over UniME, with several per-dataset regressions, e.g., Place365, Visual7W-pointing), and the absolute SCaR precision@1 values (~27-57%) indicate the benchmark/model combination is far from practically reliable, which is not thoroughly discussed.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated novelty: VIRTUE is among the first embedding models to natively support visual prompts (points, boxes, masks) by integrating a segmentation model (SAM2) with a VLM, addressing a genuine gap in text-only interactive embedding models.

Dual contribution: beyond the model, the paper introduces SCaR, a large-scale (1M sample) visual-interactive image-to-text retrieval benchmark with carefully designed GPT-4V-based negative generation (element swapping), multi-stage LLM+human filtering, and reported inter-annotator agreement (Cohen's Kappa 0.89), which shows diligence in benchmark construction.

Comprehensive evaluation: results across 36 MMEB tasks (IND and OOD) and 5 SCaR datasets, against a wide range of CLIP-based and VLM-based baselines, with consistent SOTA gains on both universal and visual-interactive tasks.

Extensive ablation and analysis: 9-way ablation (backbone, instructions, resolution, segmentation alternatives, SAM2 size, connector design, embedding length, cross-modal modeling, finetuning SAM2), hyperparameter studies, robustness analyses (jittered boxes, partial masks, random boxes/points), catastrophic-forgetting analysis after SCaR-train, and latency/memory comparisons.

Evidence that entity-level segmentation embeddings help even non-interactive tasks (MMEB +5.1 for 2B, +2.0 for 7B over strongest baselines), with the VLM2Vec comparison being a particularly fair control since it shares the training schema and data.
Reproducibility: code, models, and benchmark releases are promised; detailed training configurations (Appendix C) and prompt templates (Appendix D) are provided.
Well-organized paper with clear writing, informative figures (data pipeline, architecture), and useful qualitative case studies (I2I retrieval, on-the-fly visual hinting for VQA/I2T correction).
weaknesses: Potential circularity in benchmark design: SCaR negatives are generated by GPT-4V as caption variants resolvable only with full-image context plus visual prompts; this design may inherently favor VIRTUE's segmentation-based conditioning over baseline approaches that must textualize bounding boxes, and the paper does not deeply analyze this potential bias.

Some ground-truth captions (e.g., ADE20K) are themselves GPT-4V-generated, raising questions about annotation fidelity and whether the benchmark measures human-grounded retrieval quality; human inspection is only 'both/either flagged' removal with two inspectors, and no human performance ceiling is reported.

Absolute SCaR performance of all models (6–30 out-of-domain, ~57 in-domain) remains low, suggesting the benchmark may be very noisy or overly difficult; only precision@1 is reported, with no significance testing or multiple-seed variance for the main results.

The 2B gains (+5.1 on MMEB) versus 7B gains (+2.0) differ considerably, and some per-task wins (e.g., MMRet on retrieval baselines) are close; the paper would benefit from more discussion of when segmentation embeddings help and when they do not.

Interactive evaluation is limited to image-to-text retrieval (SCaR); interactive image-to-image retrieval is only shown as qualitative case studies on a handful of GPT-4o-generated in-the-wild examples rather than a quantitative benchmark, which weakens the I2I claims in Figure 1 and the introduction.

The instruction 'Find the caption that best describes the segmented object...' leaks task structure that baselines do not receive in an equivalent form; while the paper attempts fairness (textualized bboxes for baselines), an instruction-matched ablation for VIRTUE without visual prompts would strengthen claims (the text-only row in Tab. 11 helps but appears only in the appendix).
No discussion of compute fairness: VIRTUE adds a full SAM2 branch (~significant extra parameters and 422ms vs 139ms for cropping), and efficiency trade-offs are relegated to the appendix.
